summary: States the IETF consensus that standard protocols must use appropriate strong security mechanisms, and gives the history and rationale behind that rule. It establishes this requirement as a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This document records the rule that protocols written by the IETF must be able to keep data safe, so that the people who deploy them can switch the protection on. It does not say every protocol must encrypt everything; it says the machinery must be there.

subtitle: The IETF rule that its standard protocols must be able to provide strong security.

tldr.problem: Protocols written for a closed network end up on the open Internet anyway, and a protocol with no security in it cannot be fixed later without breaking everything built on top of it.
tldr.mechanism: The document records the IETF consensus that standard protocols must implement strong security, so that whoever deploys them can turn it on. It separates that duty to implement from the duty to use, and it explains that encryption is only one of the three security services a protocol may need.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3365 is a Best Current Practice. It sets out the reasoning and the history rather than specifying a mechanism, so the requirement it states applies to the protocols written after it.

today: RFC 3365 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted. It states a requirement and the reasoning behind it rather than specifying a mechanism, so the protocols written after it are the ones that carry the requirement in their own Security Considerations sections.

sections.title: Why IETF Standards Must Be Secure
sections.content:
The purpose of this document is to document the IETF consensus on security requirements for protocols, as well as to provide the background and motivation for them.

The Internet is a global network of independently managed networks and hosts. There is no central authority responsible for the operation of the network, and none responsible for the provision of security across it either. Security needs to be provided end to end or host to host. The IETF's security role is to ensure that IETF standard protocols have the necessary features to provide appropriate security for the application as it may be used across the Internet. Mandatory to implement mechanisms should provide adequate security to protect sensitive business applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody runs the Internet as a whole, so nobody can be trusted to protect it for you. Each protocol has to carry the means of protecting itself, because only the protocol knows what it is being used for.

sections.title: Three Security Services
sections.content:
The Internet Security Glossary provides a comprehensive listing of internetwork security services and their definitions, and the document repeats three of them.

An authentication service is a security service that verifies an identity claimed by or for an entity, be it a process, computer system or person. At the internetwork layer this includes verifying that a datagram came from where it purports to originate, and at the application layer it includes verifying that the entity performing an operation is who it claims to be.

A data confidentiality service protects data against unauthorized disclosure to unauthorized individuals or processes. The document notes that Internet Standards Documents SHOULD NOT use data confidentiality as a synonym for privacy, which is a different concept: privacy refers to the right of an entity, normally a person acting on its own behalf, to determine the degree to which it will interact with its environment, including the degree to which the entity is willing to share information about itself with others.

A data integrity service protects against unauthorized changes to data, including both intentional change, including destruction, and accidental change, including loss, by ensuring that changes to data are detectable.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things are worth protecting: who is talking to you, what you send them, and the fact that what they sent has not been altered on the way. The third one is easy to forget, but a protocol that cannot detect a changed message is not safe either.

sections.title: Enclaves and the Internet
sections.content:
The Internet provides no inherent security. Enclaves of networking exist where users believe that security is provided by the environment itself, an example being a company network not connected to the global Internet. One might imagine that protocols designed to operate in such an enclave would not require any security services, as the security is provided by the environment.

History has shown that applications that operate using the TCP/IP protocol suite wind up being used over the Internet. This is true even when the original application was not envisioned to be used in a wide area Internet environment. If an application is not designed to provide security, users of the application discover that they are vulnerable to attack.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol written for a company network that is not connected to the Internet ends up running on the Internet anyway. That is what happened repeatedly in the 1990s, and it is why a protocol cannot be designed on the assumption that its surroundings are safe.

sections.title: Using the Existing Security Toolkits
sections.content:
The IETF has several security protocols and standards. IP Security, IPsec, and Transport Layer Security, TLS, are two well known protocols. The Simple Authentication and Security Layer, SASL, and the Generic Security Service Application Programming Interface, GSSAPI, provide services within the context of a host protocol. They can be viewed as toolkits to use within another protocol.

One of the critical choices a protocol designer must make is whether to make use of one of the existing protocols, engineer their own protocol to use one of the standard tools, or do something completely different. There is no one correct answer for all protocols, and designers really need to look at the threats to their own protocol and design appropriate counter-measures.

The purpose of the Security Considerations section required to be present in an RFC on the Internet Standards Track is to provide a place for protocol designers to document the threats and explain the logic behind their security design.
sections.plainLanguage: There are already good security building blocks, so a new protocol should usually use one of them rather than invent its own. The rule that every standard RFC must have a Security Considerations section exists so that the reasoning behind the choice is written down and can be argued with.

sections.title: The Danvers Doctrine
sections.content:
At the 32cd IETF held in Danvers, Massachusetts during April of 1995, the IESG asked the plenary for a consensus on the strength of security that should be provided by IETF standards. Although the immediate issue before the IETF was whether or not to support export grade security, which is to say weak security, in standards, the question raised the generic issue of security in general. The overwhelming consensus was that the IETF should standardize on the use of the best security available, regardless of national policies. This consensus is often referred to as the Danvers Doctrine.

Over time the interpretation of the Danvers Doctrine has been extended to imply that all IETF protocols should operate securely. Since 1995 the Internet has increasingly come under attack from various malicious actors, and in 2000 significant press coverage was devoted to Distributed Denial of Service attacks. However many of these attacks were launched by first compromising an Internet connected computer system, and usually many systems are compromised in order to launch a significant distributed attack.

One of the continuing arguments against building security into protocols is the argument that a given protocol is intended only for use in protected environments where security will not be an issue. However it is very hard to predict how a protocol will be used in the future. What may be intended only for a restricted environment may well wind up being deployed in the global Internet, and we cannot wait until that point to fix security problems, because by the time we realize this deployment it is too late. The solution is that we MUST implement strong security in all protocols, to provide for the all too frequent day when the protocol comes into widespread use in the global Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: In April 1995 the IETF agreed that its standards should use the strongest security available, whatever national rules said about exporting it. The reasoning is that you cannot add security to a published protocol without breaking the software built on it, so it has to be there from the start.

sections.title: Implementing Security Is Not the Same as Using It
sections.content:
The document notes that there is a significant difference between MUST implement and MUST use. Some protocols may be deployed in secure enclaves for which security is not an issue, and security protocol processing may add a significant performance degradation. It is therefore completely reasonable for security features to be an option that the end user of the protocol may choose to disable. The document uses a fuzzy definition of end user here: not only the ultimate end user, but any deployer of a technology, which may be an entire enterprise.

However security must be a MUST implement, so that end users will have the option of enabling it when the situation calls for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing the security into the software does not mean every user has to switch it on. It means the switch is there for the people who need it, which is the whole point of putting it in from the start.

sections.title: Is Encryption Required?
sections.content:
Not necessarily, but the question needs to be made more precise. Exactly what security services are appropriate for a given protocol depends heavily on the application it is implementing. Many people assume that encryption means confidentiality, in other words the encryption of the content of protocol messages. However there are many applications where confidentiality is not a requirement, but authentication and integrity are.

One example might be a building control application using IP technology to operate heat and vent controls. There is likely no requirement to protect the confidentiality of messages that instruct heat vents to open and close. However authentication and integrity are likely important if the building is to be protected from a malicious actor raising or lowering the temperature at will.

Yet we often require cryptographic technology to implement authentication and integrity of protocol messages. So if the question is MUST we implement confidentiality, the answer will be depends. However if the question is MUST we make use of cryptographic technology, the answer is likely.

The document then addresses the resistance that the mention of cryptographic technology causes in many IETF forums. Many people seem to associate the word cryptography with concerns such as export control and performance. On export control, at least from most of the developed world, it is becoming less of a concern, and even where it is a concern the concern is not over cryptography itself but in its use in providing confidentiality. On performance, the document notes that there are issues, but that finding the appropriate way to use cryptographic technology so as to eliminate or at least minimize its impact is an engineering exercise. On understanding, you do not have to become a cryptographer in order to make effective use of cryptographic technology; instead you make use of existing well understood ciphers and cipher suites to solve the engineering problem at hand.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting everything is not the same as keeping a protocol safe. A message that turns a heating vent on does not need to be secret, but it does need to come from the right place unaltered. The document's answer is that using cryptographic machinery is usually required, but which of the three protections you need depends on the application.
